div.p: Phased execution models separate computation from access to shared resources to make task execution predictable. These task models minimize interference between tasks, making them suitable for modern complex multi-core platforms. In the phased execution model, tasks perform computations only using the local memory to avoid accessing the shared memory during task execution. All instructions and data, including the intermediate results, are stored in the local memory during execution. Thus, the local memory size becomes a crucial factor in contrast to conventional execution. In the literature, nonpreemptive and fully preemptive execution of phased execution models are studied. While the non-preemptive approaches utilize the local memory well, schedulability is reduced due to blocking. On the other hand, fully preemptive execution phases allow for better schedulability but require significantly more local memory capacity to implement preemptions at runtime without violating the model's execution semantics. Thus, this work evaluates different approaches to limited preemptive scheduling of the phased execution model under partitioned fixed-priority scheduling. We demonstrate that preemption thresholds and nonpreemptive regions can successfully be used to satisfy both timing and memory constraints of phased tasks.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: While originally proposed for single-core systems [1], phased execution models are a good solution to tame the complexity and interference in modern multi-core systems. These models separate and dedicate phases for memory transactions and computations of a task to improve predictability. We focus on the 3-phase task model, a generalized version of the PREM model [2], [3]. It separates memory operations and the execution of a task by dividing it into three phases: Read Phase (R), Execute Phase (E), and Write Phase (W). The Read phase is dedicated to reading all necessary data and code of the task from the main memory to the local memory. Next is the Execute phase, where the computations of the task are performed without accessing the shared resources. After the execution of the task, the Write phase writes the resulting data to the shared memory. Additionally, contention when accessing the main memory is avoided by not allowing two memory phases to be scheduled simultaneously.

While non-preemptive scheduling is often used for phased execution models, the blocking times in non-preemptive scheduling can be avoided by allowing preemption. Since the tasks' execution phase is performed by only accessing the local memory in the phased execution model, in preemptive systems, the local data of the preempted task must be carefully handled during preemption. Two methods are found in the literature for this purpose: 1) the overhead minimizing (Keep in Core) method and 2) the waiting time minimizing (Write Back) method [4]. The first method keeps the preempted task's local data in the core's local memory during preemption. In contrast, the second method writes back the data of the preempted task to the main memory and reads again once its execution is resumed by scheduling an additional write phase and a read phase, respectively.

In this ongoing work, we focus on fixed-priority scheduling for partitioned systems. The Keep in Core method suits partitioned systems better than the Write Back method, as preempted tasks always resume execution on the same core after preemption. However, with this preemption approach, the task set must not only be schedulable but also satisfy local memory constraints to be feasible [5]. Consider the example tasks assigned to the same core shown in Figure 2 where the local memory capacity is 32KB. While the task set is not schedulable with non-preemptive scheduling (Figure 2a), with fully preemptive execute phases, all tasks meet their deadlines (Figure 2b). However, the task set does not satisfy local memory constraints with fully preemptive execute phases as all three tasks are involved in preemption at the same time, exceeding the local memory capacity, i.e., 33KB > 32KB, which makes the task set infeasible.

Yao et al. [6] and Melani et al. [7], [8] also have highlighted possible benefits of limited preemption methods to address the drawbacks due to the limitation of the local memory. While a detailed investigation has been mentioned as future work, to the best of our knowledge, it has not been done yet. Thilakasiri et al. [4] investigated different preemption approaches for the phased execution model and also provided the key observation that limited preemption can benefit phased tasks significantly more than fully and non-preemptive scheduling using timetriggered scheduling. In contrast, this work focuses on online scheduling. All of these motivate us further to explore limited preemption methods for the phase execution model. While many works have proposed different limited preemption methods for conventional tasks [9], [10], there has not been much explicit work on limited preemption for the phased execution model. Preemption points is a well-known limited preemption solution. The tasks are split into several non-preemptive subjobs where preemption is only allowed at the boundaries of these sub-jobs [11]. Applicationspecific preemption points can be selected by looking at the programs of tasks to improve the benefit of preemption points. Though the objective is different, this has been explored by the works that exist in the literature for splitting 3-phase tasks [13]. Similar to preemption points, these methods also split the task into several non-preemptive subjobs by looking at the task program. Preemption thresholds [14] and deferred preemption [15] are two other well-known limited preemption approaches. Out of these approaches, the area of preemption points has been subject to previous work. Additionally, it requires details of the tasks program. Therefore, in this ongoing work, we focus on strategies to configure preemption thresholds and methods to introduce an initial non-preemptive section to execute a section of the execution phase non-preemptively.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL A. Platform Model
div.p: We consider a multi-core system where each core has its private, local memory, i.e., scratch-pad memory (SPM) of size S. This local memory stores the data and instructions needed to execute the tasks assigned to its core. All cores can access the main memory via a shared interconnect, e.g., a bus.

div.head: B. Application Model
div.p: The considered application consists of a set of n independent, periodic tasks τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n }. Each task is divided into three phases, i.e., the Read phase, the Execution phase, and the Write phase, and are respectively dedicated to read, execute, and write operations of a task. In the R-phase, all the data and instructions of the task are copied from the main memory to the local memory of the core. Thus, the following E-phase is executed only using local data copies of the task. This means that the inter-core contention is removed by avoiding accessing the main memory during computations.

Once the E-phase is completed, the W-phase writes back the resulting data to the main memory. Each task is represented using the tuple (T i , D i , M i , P i , O i , C r i , C e i , C w i ). T i and D i represent the task's period and deadline, respectively where D i ≤ T i . M i is the memory footprint of the task. It is considered to be the sum of the code size (Im i ), total data size (Dm i ), and the maximum stack usage (M s i ) of the task, i.e., M i = Im i + Dm i + M s i . P i represents the task's fixed priority. O i represents the initial offset of the task. C r i , C e i , and C w i respectively represent the execution times for the read, execute, and write phases. The total execution time C i is their sum, i.e., C i = C r i + C e i + C w i . The utilization of a task can be represented as u i = C i /T i , where the total utilization of the task set is n i=1 u i .

div.head: C. Execution Model
div.p: Partitioned fixed-priority scheduling is used. A task's read and write phases are non-preemptive, while execution phases can be preempted. The tasks are scheduled from the memory perspective. Pending read and write phases of a core are ordered according to their priorities to be scheduled. To avoid contention when accessing the shared memory, only one memory phase is allowed to be active at a time. Thus, the highest priority pending memory phase out of all cores (global) is scheduled on the bus, where it will then run to completion (non-preemptive). The execute phase of a task starts directly upon its read phase's completion. This model is in line with related work [12].

In this paper, we consider the Keep in Core preemption method [4], where the data of the preempted task is kept in the core's local memory during preemption until it resumes execution (see Figure 1). τ 1 , shown in yellow in Figure 1 is the preempted task and τ 2 , shown in purple is the preempting task. At the time of preemption, the execution of the preempted task is paused, and the read phase of the preempting task is started. Once all 3 phases of τ 2 are completed, τ 1 's execution phase can resume. The bottom part of Figure 1 shows the memory usage of the tasks before and during preemption compared to the total memory capacity of the core, S. The local memory is considered as one single partition. It can be managed as a stack. The last task to come finishes the first. Importantly, data of both preempting and preempted tasks must fit in the local memory, i.e., M 1 + M 2 ≤ S.

div.head: III. LIMITED PREEMPTION METHODS FOR PHASED EXECUTION MODEL
div.p: We exemplify the benefits of two limited preemptive scheduling approaches when applied to the phased execution model compared to non-or fully preemptive approaches. For each limited preemption method, we briefly discuss the benefits and which factors to consider when selecting their parameters.

div.head: A. Motivation
div.p: Consider the tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 in the example mapped to the same core. Figure 2 depicts their schedules and memory usage over time using non-preemptive (Figure 2a), fully preemptive E-phases (Figure 2b) and two limited preemptive scheduling methods. Figure 2c and 2d depict the schedules respectively when only a section of the execution phase is preemptive and when preemption thresholds are used. In both non-preemptive and fully-preemptive scheduling, either the schedulability or the memory constraints can suffer due to blocking times and unnecessary preemptions, respectively. Whereas in both limited preemption cases, the tasks meet their deadlines, and the memory constraints are satisfied as only two Fig. 2. tasks occupy the local memory simultaneously. Therefore, this example demonstrates that limited preemption can improve the feasibility of task sets. The two limited preemption approaches are discussed in the following sections.

div.head: B. Preemption Thresholds
div.p: The preemption threshold method reduces the number of preemptions by avoiding preemption from lower-priority tasks than a threshold priority [14]. Each task, τ i , is assigned a nominal priority and a preemption threshold, θ i . When this method is applied to the 3-phase model, a task's priority is increased to its preemption threshold once it starts its read phase. This means that a task's nominal priority is used when scheduling its read phase. A task can only be preempted by a task whose nominal priority is more than the preemption threshold during the preemptive E-phase. The priority is kept at the preemption threshold until its write phase is completed. However, it is important to highlight that the preemption threshold only affects the local tasks that are mapped to the same core. Thus, when a write phase is waiting to be scheduled, its preemption threshold is used to decide which task has the highest priority locally, while its nominal priority is used globally when deciding access to the bus.

The example Figure 2d shows how assigning preemption thresholds helps to reduce the memory requirement of the tasks to 24KB compared to the 33KB when fully preemptive E-phases are used (Figure 2b). The preemption threshold of τ 2 is raised to the same priority level as τ 1 so that τ 2 cannot be preempted by τ 1 . Thus, unlike when fully preemptive E-phases are used, 1 st instance of τ 2 is not preempted at t = 5 by τ 1 , avoiding all three tasks utilizing the local memory simultaneously. This effect is similar to that of creating nonpreemptive groups, a method proposed for stack-sharing in real-time operating systems (RTOS) [16]. In the ongoing work, we look at methods to utilize non-preemptive groups for phased tasks to improve their feasibility by configuring priorities and preemption thresholds.

div.head: C. Configuring a non-preemptive section
div.p: This section introduces a limited preemption method that configures a non-preemptive section in the execution phase rather than allowing the complete length of the tasks execution phase to be preemptive. The initial idea is to configure a non-preemptive section at the beginning of the E-phase, prolonging the non-preemptive read phase. Thus, no preemption is allowed between the read phase and this E-phase nonpreemptive section (see τ 3 in Figure 2c). For each task τ i , the length of the non-preemptive section, np i , can vary in the range [0, C e i ]. When np i = 0, the task's execution phase is executed fully preemptively, and the execution phase is executed non-preemptively when np i = C e i . Figure 2c shows how a non-preemptive section can help to reduce the memory requirement. A 3-time-unit non-preemptive section is configured to extend the non-preemptive read phase of τ 3 . Thus, in total, τ 3 executes its first 6 time units non-preemptively. By doing this, all three tasks being involved in preemption at the same time is avoided.

The deferred preemption model has some similarities to this idea. In the deferred preemption model, a maximum nonpreemptive section is defined for each task. Preemption by a higher priority task will be postponed by this maximum non-preemptive section length. The maximum non-preemptive section is defined from the perspective of the preempting task by finding the maximum blocking times each preempting task can tolerate [15]. With the proposed initial non-preemptive section, the length of the non-preemptive section and its start and end times are determined before runtime. In contrast, in the deferred preemption model, the start and end times of the non-preemptive sections are unknown at design times and are assumed to occur at the worst possible time in analysis. Thus, a fixed, non-preemptive section at the beginning of the execution phase of the task is more predictable and easier to implement.

When calculating the length of an initial non-preemptive section for tasks, the problem must be looked at from two sides to ensure that all tasks in the task set meet their deadlines. 1) from the perspective of the preempting task, the maximum amount of blocking that can be tolerated, including the nonpreemptive read phase times, and 2) from the perspective of the preempted task, the interference (paused time) due to preemption until execution is resumed must be compared with its own slack time.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: While the phased execution model makes task execution on multi-core platforms more predictable, its execution semantics make preemption non-trivial as local memory is solely used during task computation. Given local memory's typical limited capacity on COTS platforms, the satisfaction of memory constraints must be accounted for in feasibility checks. Limited preemption is identified as a good candidate to improve feasibility by satisfying both timing and memory constraints. In this paper, we explored existing limited preemption methods and their applicability to the phased execution model. Strategies to assign preemption thresholds and configure nonpreemptive sections are ongoing/ future work. To evaluate task set feasibility under these approaches, we plan to adapt an existing memory analysis and WCRT analysis.
